claim: A single deployable humanoid control policy, switched between skills by a command input, can perform several different ball skills (trapping, dribbling, shooting) and chain them into long sequences, then carry over from simulation to a real robot, if during training each skill gets its own motion-style discriminator and its own value estimate and the policy's history encoder is trained to estimate the robot's and ball's velocities. Supported only if, under the same task rewards, reference motions and maximum training budget, its full-sequence success is at least 15 points higher than the best single-stage multi-skill baseline on both a two-skill sequence (dribble then shoot) and a five-stage sequence (trap, three dribbles through waypoints, shoot); and if on the physical humanoid it succeeds in at least 60% of trials on each of four tasks, two of them skill sequences, where a standard motion-prior controller succeeds in at most 10%.

experiments: Set up training and the policy interface. Setup: PPO in Isaac Lab (policy 50 Hz, simulation 200 Hz) for the 25-DoF Noetix E1; human soccer motions captured with motion capture and retargeted with PHC; actor input is a 5-step history of proprioception, robot-relative ball and target positions and a skill command that is one-hot and linearly interpolated over 0.1 s during switches; the critic additionally sees privileged velocities and foot contacts. Each skill has its own least-squares adversarial motion discriminator (segments spanning switches excluded) and its own value head on a shared trunk, blended by the command during switches; a causal transformer encodes the history with a Barlow-Twins consistency loss and a head predicting root and ball velocity. Training adds failure-weighted command sampling, a curriculum shortening command durations from 5-10 s to 0.2-10 s, and randomised ball mass, friction and restitution.

Fix the evaluation tasks and baselines. Setup: on a quarter-scale field with randomisation and observation corruption off, atomic tasks over 100 trials: trap (ball 1-2 m away at 0.5-1.5 m/s, success if speed drops below 0.3 m/s within 20 s), dribble (ball to a target 4.5-5.5 m ahead within 20 s), shoot (from 4-6 m, ball crosses the goal line within 15 s); composite tasks over 1,000 sequential trials with commands switched by an event-based scheduler: Medium = dribble then shoot within 30 s, Hard = trap, dribble through three S-route waypoints, shoot within 40 s; substage success is conditional on reaching the stage. Baselines with identical robot, rewards, motions, observations and budget: task-reward-only PPO, AMP with one shared discriminator, conditional AMP with a latent skill reward, mixture-of-experts AMP with top-1 routing, and AMP with a mixture-of-experts history encoder.

Check the individual skills first. Result: shoot / trap / dribble success 95 / 100 / 100% against 87 / 99 / 94% for AMP; task-reward-only PPO traps (97%) but fails at shooting (9%) and dribbling (5%), and conditional and mixture-of-experts AMP fail at shooting (1%) and mostly at dribbling (8%, 36%).

Run the skill sequences. Result: Medium overall success 88.0% against 67.2% for the mixture-of-experts-encoder AMP, 51.0% for AMP, 42.6% for mixture-of-experts AMP, 11.2% for conditional AMP and 0% for PPO, with 12.0 s mean completion; Hard 81.7% against 45.6%, 27.4%, 5.0%, 0% and 0%. Substage rates show AMP losing reliability over the waypoint dribbles and final shot (52.0% and 52.6%), and the encoder baseline dribbling well (95.7%) but shooting poorly (47.6%), while the proposed policy keeps 100% dribbling and 81.7% shooting.

Remove each training component. Setup: overall Medium / Hard success with one discriminator for all skills, one shared critic, no command-duration curriculum, and five history variants (raw stacked history fed to the actor, MLP encoder with the auxiliary losses, no ball-velocity target, no velocity targets, plain MLP history encoder). Result: full 88.0 / 81.7%; one discriminator 79.5 / 79.3%; one critic 82.5 / 65.0%; no curriculum 85.5 / 30.4%; raw history 49.0 / 20.0%; MLP encoder 61.9 / 47.6%; no ball-velocity target 83.6 / 44.4%; no velocity targets 79.7 / 15.8%; plain history encoder 78.0 / 32.6%. Most components matter mainly on the long sequence; raw history drops shooting to 16% even on the atomic task.

Check that trapping success does not hinge on a lenient definition. Setup: count success only if, within 3 s of first contact (ball within 0.4 m), the ball stays below 0.25 m/s and within 0.5 m of the robot for at least 0.5 s; 100 trials per method. Result: 63.0% against 31.0% for AMP, 24.0% for conditional AMP and 50.0% for mixture-of-experts AMP, still best but far below the 100% under the lenient criterion.

Deploy on the physical humanoid. Setup: Noetix E1 with motion capture (Motive at 120 Hz via VRPN, low-pass filtered, stale data rejected) giving robot pose and ball and goal positions in the same robot-relative interface as simulation; four tasks over 10 trials each: dribble to a target region, shoot at the goal, two-step dribble with a direction change, dribble then shoot (commands switched manually); success requires no fall and the ball staying in bounds; standard AMP as baseline. Result: 8/10, 8/10, 7/10 and 6/10 against 1/10, 1/10, 0/10 and 0/10. A feasibility test with a head-mounted ZED2i camera and YOLOv8 ball detection, trained with delayed, intermittent and noisy object observations, shows ball interaction without motion capture but is not scored.
